goal:
Make `slugify` in `src/slugify.js` turn Latin letters with diacritics into plain ASCII: `slugify("Crème Brûlée")` returns `"creme-brulee"` and `slugify("Łódź")` returns `"lodz"`.

This covers every Latin letter, not only those Unicode can split into a base letter and an accent: letters with a stroke and ligatures take their usual ASCII spelling (for example `ø` → `o`, `æ` → `ae`, `ß` → `ss`). Accents count whether the title writes them precomposed or as separate combining marks after the letter.

Keep everything that works today. In particular, letters of other scripts stay exactly as they are: `slugify` keeps Cyrillic, Greek, Japanese, and every other script unchanged, apart from lower case.

constraints: Change as few files as possible.
Delete or simplify existing code before you add code.
Write a failing test that reproduces the problem before you change any source file.

candidates.approach: Add a Latin-only normalization helper inside src/slugify.js. Identify Latin letters together with their following combining marks, canonically decompose those sequences, remove their accents, and map Latin letters that do not decompose to explicit ASCII spellings such as ł→l, ø→o, æ→ae, and ß→ss. Generate or audit the exception table against the full Unicode Latin repertoire rather than stopping at common European characters. Leave non-Latin sequences untouched and retain the existing lowercase, separator-collapse, and edge-trimming behavior.
candidates.firstStep: Add regression tests for the existing slug behavior, the requested examples, decomposed Latin accents, stroke letters and ligatures, and non-Latin text—including accented Greek—to establish that normalization must be script-scoped.

candidates.approach: Implement a complete, checked-in Latin-to-ASCII mapping module and use direct code-point substitution before the existing slug cleanup, without runtime Unicode decomposition. Derive mappings from maintained transliteration data, review coverage against Unicode Latin letters, and explicitly consume combining accents following Latin letters. This trades a larger data asset and maintenance burden for predictable, reviewable behavior and avoids normalizing other scripts.
candidates.firstStep: Inventory the Unicode Latin repertoire and select a versioned, license-compatible transliteration dataset from which to generate the mapping and a coverage report.

candidates.approach: Delegate Latin transliteration to an established dependency, but wrap it with script-aware segmentation in slugify so the dependency sees only Latin letters and their attached combining marks. Pass all other text through unchanged, then apply the existing lowercase and slug-cleanup pipeline. Evaluate the dependency's full Latin coverage, expansion spellings, license, and package impact; reject any integration that transliterates Greek, Cyrillic, Japanese, or other scripts globally.
candidates.firstStep: Inspect the project's dependency and runtime constraints, then benchmark candidate transliteration libraries against a Latin-coverage fixture and mixed-script preservation tests.

candidates.approach: Build a generated, Latin-scoped transliteration rule engine rather than a decomposition helper or direct character table. Compile maintained transliteration rules into a longest-match trie or equivalent matcher that recognizes both individual Latin letters and multi-code-point accented sequences, emits ASCII replacements, and otherwise preserves the input. This explores sequence-aware transliteration and build-time generation, though its tooling and rule complexity are likely excessive for a small slug utility.
candidates.firstStep: Prototype a rule compiler and matcher with rules for precomposed and decomposed é, ł, æ, and ß, plus mixed-script fixtures, before expanding to a complete Latin rule set.
